response.internal_assessment: I am operating at L3_CONSUME — the car question has graduated from intellectual curiosity to a real financial decision I am circling. L0 and L1 are secure: 52-month runway, $117K in savings, full insurance coverage, mortgage is the only commitment. No threat below L3. The economy softening (spending index 73, unemployment ticking up) does not threaten me directly — I am retired and my pension income does not depend on local employment — but it confirms that being careful with money is not paranoia. The $281/month car payment is real money. I am evaluating whether the car still makes sense, not from fear, but from a growing suspicion that I am paying for a safety blanket I may not need.
response.inbox_interpretation: RoboRide is still running — it is not a flash in the pan. The service exists, I used it, and the price held. That matters to me. The economic indicators are mildly alarming in the abstract — 7% unemployment is not a crisis but it is a signal that the town is under stress — but they do not change my personal situation. I notice that spending is down broadly, which tells me other people are being cautious. My normalcy bias wants me to just keep the car and not think about it. But I took a real ride in tick 2 and I know the app works. I know the vehicle was clean. I know I felt fine at the end of it. The 2am fear is still there, but I find myself wondering: is RoboRide available at 2am? I do not actually know. That is a specific question I can answer.

chosen_actions.description: Call Priya Sharma, my insurance agent neighbor, and ask a specific question: what would my monthly costs look like if I dropped the car — what happens to my auto insurance premium, and is there any renter or homeowner rider that would change? I am not telling her I am selling the car. I am getting information. I will also call the RoboRide customer line or check the app to confirm whether the service runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week — specifically whether a ride at 2am to a hospital emergency room is a thing I could actually book.

resources.detail: Requesting insurance cost information — no transaction, just a phone call between neighbors

chosen_actions.reasoning: I have used RoboRide once. The test ride confirmed the technology works and I can operate it. What I do not have yet is the complete financial picture of what car ownership is actually costing me versus what regular RoboRide use would cost. And I have one specific fear — the 2am emergency — that I have not verified against reality. Before I make any decision about the car, I need those two data points. Calling Priya costs nothing and she is a neighbor I see regularly. This is the methodical next step, not a dramatic action. I am not selling the car. I am doing the homework that any sensible person would do before selling a car.

response.inner_monologue: I took the ride. It was fine — more than fine, actually. The car is sitting in the driveway and I am paying for it every month whether I use it or not. But I am not going to sell it because I took one Thursday afternoon trip to the community center. That would be impulsive, and impulsive is not who I am. What I can do is find out what I am actually paying for the car in total and whether the thing I am most afraid of — being stranded at 2am with a health emergency — is even a real risk with RoboRide or just a story I am telling myself. I owe myself that much due diligence before I decide either way.
